# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment does valuable forensic work, and most of its specific corrections are sound. The attrition finding in particular is a real discovery that the working paper misdescribed. But the conclusion goes well beyond the analysis. Nothing in the paper shows the residual per-hour gain is zero. The claim is extended from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" generally. And the comment cites the Varden trial selectively, ignoring the stratum that contradicts its conclusion.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures reproduce exactly:
- **Actual hours:** 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%), and 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%).
- **Corrected gains in Table 2:** 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%, and 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8%.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 ≈ −2.6%.
- **Other figures:** the manager-versus-records gap of 3.8 points, the retail fall of 6.9%, and the "six-point" hours overstatement (20 − 14.1).

Three figures do not check out.

**1. The hours decomposition doesn't sum.** Starting from 32 scheduled hours, "+0.7 hours per day" over four days plus 1.6 hours on the day off gives 32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = 36.4 hours, not the reported 34.6. The figures reconcile almost exactly if it is +0.7 hours *per week*: 32 + 0.3 (the baseline overhang) + 0.7 + 1.6 = 34.6. "Per day" is probably an error, and it should be checked against the logs.

**2. The energy extrapolation reaches baseline at about month 9, not "around month ten".** A straight line through 0.61 SD at month three and 0.29 SD at month six falls 0.107 SD per month and reaches zero at about month 8.7. More fundamentally, a linear extrapolation from two points carries no information about whether the decline continues or plateaus.

**3. Two of the nine exit reasons are unaccounted for.** Six gave workload and two gave scheduling, which leaves one unexplained.

## 1. The abstract misdescribes what was corrected

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems, including attrition, reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 does not correct for attrition at all. Its 17 organisations are all survivors. The 10.8% corrects only the output measure and the hours denominator.

The contribution of attrition is never quantified, yet the conclusion lists it first among the problems that account for the gain. The microdata may allow a real correction:
- the seven organisations that withdrew after starting the reduced schedule may have one or two months of output data, which would support an intention-to-treat estimate;
- failing that, bounds could be computed under explicit assumptions about how the withdrawers would have performed.

## 2. No analysis supports "entirely an artifact"

The most-corrected estimate is still a gain of +10.8%. It has no confidence interval, and no test shows it is distinguishable from zero, or that zero is plausible. A per-hour gain of zero would require record-based output of about 86 in the 17-organisation subset, not the observed 95.4.

The step from "about 11% remains" to "entirely an artifact" rests on the novelty argument alone (section 2.3). The authors themselves note in the Data note that the subsets are not representative. Yet the abstract and conclusion generalise to "reduced-hours schemes", not just this pilot.

## 3. The novelty argument is not tested, though the data to test it exist

- **The output trajectory is never examined.** Energy is a self-report, not output, so its decline does not show that productivity declined. The output index was collected monthly, and the 23 organisations have records. The direct test is to check whether output per actual hour declined from month 1 to month 6. Without it, novelty is a hypothesis rather than a finding.
- **The Varden trial bears directly on the claim.** Varden measured per-hour gains at nine months, against a control group, with record-based output and timesheet hours. That design rules out exactly the measurement and selection problems the comment identifies. The persistence of its gains to month 9 does not refute novelty, but the comment should engage with it.
- **"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter"** is a rhetorical move, not evidence. It is legitimate to say six months cannot distinguish the two explanations. It is not legitimate to then conclude in favour of one of them.

## 4. Varden is cited selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature". It does not mention Varden's case-processing stratum from the same trial, which found:
- output per employee of −2.1% (CI −6.8 to +2.6);
- output per actual hour of +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4).

That is a randomised, record-based, actual-hours estimate of a per-hour gain, so it directly contradicts "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty". A balanced comment needs to address it, perhaps by arguing that case-processing gains are demand-limited or will fade by month 24.

## 5. The critique of the meetings analysis mischaracterises Varden

**The seven offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known".** They are the entire treated case-processing stratum. The meeting data were collected at month six at managers' request, which Varden reports.

**Varden did not present meetings as an established mechanism.** It stated that the analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, could not establish a mechanism, and that a confirmatory test was registered for month 24. The comment's caution is fair, but it is aimed at a claim Varden did not make.

**The meetings hypothesis cuts against the novelty argument.** If per-hour gains come from removing low-value meeting time, that is a structural change with no reason to fade. Varden's own figures suggest meeting cuts could account for most of its case-processing per-hour gain. The comment should acknowledge that the mechanism it dismisses is an alternative to novelty.

## 6. Weaknesses in the corrections themselves

**Record-based output is not automatically valid.**
- "Billable hours delivered" is one of the record types. As an output measure it is itself tied to hours worked, so it mechanically falls when hours fall.
- The record types differ across organisations and were not seasonally adjusted.

The manager-versus-records gap is persuasive: 19 of 23 organisations in the same direction has a one-sided sign-test p ≈ 0.001. But "records = truth" needs defending, and the −3.8 needs a confidence interval.

**Revenue deflation.** CPI is a rough deflator for these organisations' output prices. The real-terms point is fair, but "approximately −2.6%" implies more precision than CPI allows.

**Weighting.** The working paper used employee-weighted means. The comment does not say how the subset figures were weighted, so the rows of Table 2 may not be comparable.

## 7. Per-hour and per-employee conflated in the conclusion

"Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" is a per-employee finding. Both prior papers already agree on it. It is not evidence against per-hour gains, which is the claim the comment says it refutes. Varden makes exactly this distinction, and this comment loses it in its final paragraph.

## What the comment establishes

- **Attrition was misdescribed.** The working paper said organisations withdrew during preparation; in fact most withdrew after the schedule began, mostly citing workload. This is a significant finding that the Halden authors should correct.
- **Manager ratings ran high.** They exceeded records by about 4 points, consistently across organisations.
- **Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.** This is consistent with Varden's 13–17%.
- **The headline gain falls sharply with correction.** It drops from about 23% to about 11% in the subset where both corrections are possible.
- **Revenue fell in real terms.**
- **The sector-general claim was an artifact of the metric.** The comment's point here matches what I noted in my review of the working paper.

## What it does not establish

It does not show that the residual gain is zero, that it is a novelty effect, or that per-hour gains from reduced hours in general are artifacts. Varden's case-processing result is the main counter-evidence, and it is not addressed.

A defensible conclusion would read roughly: *the Halden pilot overstated per-hour gains by more than half; the corrected estimate of about 11% comes from a non-random subset of survivors with no comparison group, and six months cannot distinguish a durable effect from novelty*. That is a strong and useful result without the overreach.
